Subject: Acme TCO post-call recap & next steps

Hi Sahil / Priya 

Thanks again for the time today. Quick recap of what we heard and the recommended next steps from Redwood to get you a concrete TCO/ROI comparison you can take to procurement.

Key pain points you mentioned:
- Token spend is the primary driver of your ML infra costs (spiky nightly batch calls + real-time web traffic).
- Tight budget target (~$50k/month) for inference across primary product features.
- Need to keep P95 latency under ~200ms for interactive flows.

Goals we agreed on:
1) Establish current-end baseline (monthly tokens, per-token cost) and Redwood-managed TCO.
2) Identify levers (batching, KV/prefix caching, quantization & model selection, reserved capacity) to hit target budget while preserving quality.
3) Propose a pilot scope and timeline (3-month pilot with targeted query set + eval).

High-level TCO (back-of-envelope using call assumptions):
- Monthly tokens (est): 1.2B tokens
- Current spend (estimated): ~$0.10/token effective (incl. 3rd party managed hosting + inefficiencies) -> ~$120k/month
- Redwood optimized (batching + prefix caching + q4 quantized model path): estimated cost ~$48k/month (~60% reduction).

Primary assumptions for the model (we'll confirm with your telemetry):
- Avg prompt tokens: 95
- Avg response tokens: 320
- Effective prefix-match caching reduces generated tokens by ~18% for your use case (docs/Q&A heavy).
- Continuous batching and dynamic batching reclaim ~25-35% of per-token compute cost for your traffic shape.
- Quantized model variants (q4) reduce GPU consumption and cost per token with minor latency tradeoffs.

Attachments: ACME-TCO-model-v1.xlsx (attached) — includes line-by-line assumptions so you can tweak token counts, QPS, cache hit rates, and reserved capacity pricing.

Next steps / asks:
- Sahil: can you confirm the monthly token volume (or give us a 3-week sample access) and the SLA targets you must meet?
- Priya: what's your procurement timeline & any PO/contract requirements we should be aware of?
- Rafael + I will iterate the TCO spreadsheet and propose a 60–90 minute procurement + technical alignment meeting next week.

If it helps, Rafael can run the pilot sizing and capacity estimate.

Thanks — looking forward to aligning on the numbers.

Best,

Thanks Marissa — helpful recap. A few clarifying questions so we can validate the spreadsheet assumptions before sharing with Finance: 

1) Cache assumptions — when you say ~18% token reduction via prefix caching, is that applied to prompt tokens, response tokens, or both? How are you modeling dynamic (user-specific) prefixes vs static doc prefixes?

2) Batching savings — is the 25-35% reduction assuming dedicated reserved capacity or just hosted (shared) with continuous batching? We have pretty spiky ingests during batch windows so curious how that impacts avg savings.

3) Model family — which model(s) did you use for the estimate (size/quantization) and what's the fallback policy for the 1–2% of queries that need higher fidelity?

4) Procurement — our finance team will need an estimated contract value and whether there are minimum commitment terms to get the quoted reserved pricing. Priya, can you share any constraints on term/commitments?

If you can update the spreadsheet with the prompt/response split and footnote the caching application, that would help get this into our internal review. Happy to jump on a follow-up call after that.

—Sahil

Hi Sahil — great questions. Quick answers and I updated the attached model with more explicit assumptions (see ACME-TCO-model-v1-updated.xlsx).

1) Caching — applied primarily to generated tokens (responses) where we see repeated prefixes from knowledge-base style Q&A. For Acme's query mix we modeled: 12% prompt savings, 18% response savings, combined effective reduction ~16% overall token spend. We included a conservative TTL of 24 hours for document caches and show a sensitivity table for 0–72h. Dynamic user-specific prefixes are excluded from caching by default in the model, but we can run an eval on a sample dataset to estimate incremental cacheability.

2) Batching savings — the 25-35% figure assumes reserved capacity / dedicated pools with continuous batching optimizations. On shared hosted instances you still get batching gains but they are lower (~10-15%) due to mixed workload boundaries. For your heavy nightly batch windows we recommend a small dedicated pool (bursting to hosted) to preserve latency for interactive flows while maintaining batch efficiency overnight. The updated model includes a dedicated capacity line with monthly reserved pricing.

3) Model family & fallback — base estimate uses redwood-2b-q4 for the bulk of requests. For 1–2% of high-fidelity queries we model a fallback to redwood-13b (on-demand) which raises cost for those requests but keeps overall blended cost within target. The spreadsheet includes per-model cost-per-1M-token rows so you can toggle the mix.

4) Procurement / commitments — reserved pricing in the model is shown as a monthly committed spend (12-month) and a pay-as-you-go hosted line for burst/overflow. Rafael is cc'd and will follow up with exact contractual minimums; short answer: to achieve the ~60% reduction we modeled requires a modest 6–12 month commitment at the reserved tier; we spelled out a pilot contract option in the notes.

ROI note: using your current forecast, we estimate payback time on integration + pilot engineering work at ~3 months (based on reduced monthly spend + avoided infra ops). The updated spreadsheet has an ROI tab.

Next steps: 
- Rafael: can you propose 2 slots for a joint procurement + architecture run-through next week (we'll include Priya)?
- Sahil: if you can share a 2–3 week sample of token telemetry (or grant a read-only view) Rafael and I will replace the back-of-envelope counts with actuals and re-run the model.

Attachment: ACME-TCO-model-v1-updated.xlsx (Excel spreadsheet, 145KB)
